items.title: CNN, Politico and MS NOW Sue Trump Administration Over White House Press Credential Ban
items.body:
## Three Newsrooms, One Legal Fight

CNN, Politico and MS NOW filed a joint lawsuit against the Trump administration this week after the White House revoked press credentials for reporters from all three outlets, cutting off their access to the briefing room, press pool rotations and other official events held on White House grounds.

The outlets argue in their complaint that stripping credentials from working journalists without a clear, individualized justification violates the First Amendment's protections for a free press, as well as the Fifth Amendment's guarantee of due process. Their filing asks a federal court to restore the reporters' access while the case proceeds and, ultimately, to bar the administration from using credentialing decisions to punish outlets over the content of their coverage.

## What the Ban Actually Changed

Losing a White House credential is not a symbolic penalty. It determines whether a reporter can walk into the briefing room, join the small rotating "pool" that travels with the president, or ask a question at a press conference. For CNN, Politico and MS NOW, the ban means their correspondents now have to rely on pooled footage and reporting from other outlets to cover the presidency — a significant handicap for organizations built around original, on-the-ground reporting.

The White House has not laid out a detailed public rationale for singling out these three newsrooms. In past disputes over press access, administration officials have generally pointed to conduct during briefings or the tone of an outlet's coverage as justification, arguments that press advocates say amount to viewpoint discrimination dressed up as an access policy.

## A Fight the Courts Have Seen Before

This is not the first time a White House has tried to control the press corps by revoking credentials, and history has not been kind to the practice. In 1977, a federal court ruled in *Sherrill v. Knight* that the government cannot deny a reporter a White House pass without notice, a reason and a chance to respond — establishing that access, once broadly granted to the press corps, can't be pulled arbitrarily. During Trump's first term, a federal judge sided with CNN in 2018 after correspondent Jim Acosta's credential was suspended, ordering it restored on due-process grounds.

Legal experts note that this precedent puts the administration in a difficult position: courts have consistently held that once the White House opens its doors to the press generally, it cannot then pick and choose which outlets get to walk through them based on how officials feel about their coverage.

## The Stakes Beyond Three Newsrooms

Press freedom organizations, including the Committee to Protect Journalists and the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, have voiced support for the outlets, framing the case as a test of whether any administration can use credentialing as a tool to reward friendly coverage and punish critical reporting. Other news organizations are watching closely, since a ruling either way could shape how future administrations — of any party — manage access to the White House press corps.

For now, CNN, Politico and MS NOW say they intend to keep covering the White House using whatever tools remain available to them while the lawsuit moves through the courts. A hearing date has not yet been set, but legal observers expect the outlets to seek expedited relief given the ongoing impact on their day-to-day coverage.

*This article summarizes publicly reported developments and is intended for general news information purposes.*

items.title: 120 Days, Every City: Inside the FCC's Push to Set a National Clock on Broadband Permits
items.body:
## A National Deadline for Local Permits

The Federal Communications Commission is considering a sweeping change to how broadband infrastructure gets approved across the United States: a uniform 120-day "shot clock" that would require local and state governments to act on permit applications for telecom buildouts within that window, or risk having the permit considered automatically granted. The proposal would also cap the fees municipalities can charge companies to access public rights-of-way — the sidewalks, utility poles, and roadways where fiber lines and small-cell equipment are installed.

Federal officials backing the plan frame it as a response to a persistent complaint from telecom and internet providers: that inconsistent, sometimes years-long local review processes are one of the biggest bottlenecks slowing the rollout of faster, more reliable internet service, particularly in underserved and rural communities. Supporters argue that a predictable national timeline would let companies plan builds with more certainty and reduce the cost of expansion, savings they say could eventually be passed on to consumers.

## Why Cities Are Pushing Back

Local governments and organizations representing them, including groups that speak for thousands of cities and counties nationwide, have raised strong objections. Their core argument is one of authority: rights-of-way have traditionally been managed locally because it is local officials who deal with the practical consequences of construction — torn-up streets, utility conflicts, safety inspections, and coordination with other infrastructure projects like water and sewer work.

Critics of the proposal warn that a rigid 120-day deadline does not account for the wide variation in review complexity across different jurisdictions. A small town with a part-time planning staff and a dense historic downtown may need more time to properly vet an application than a large city with a dedicated permitting department. Municipal advocates also worry that capping fees below what it actually costs a city to review applications and maintain public infrastructure could shift those costs onto local taxpayers instead of the companies benefiting from access to public property.

There is also a practical enforcement question. If a permit is treated as automatically approved after 120 days regardless of whether a review was completed, some local officials fear that could reduce leverage to negotiate basic safeguards, such as requirements to repair streets after construction or coordinate work to avoid repeated digging in the same location.

## The Industry Perspective

Telecom and broadband trade groups have generally welcomed the proposal, describing permitting delays as a genuine obstacle to closing the digital divide, especially in the context of federal and state programs designed to expand high-speed internet access to unserved areas. They argue that in many cases, local reviews take far longer than necessary not because of legitimate complexity, but because of understaffed permitting offices, unclear application requirements, or, in some instances, an incentive to extract higher fees before granting approval.

Industry representatives point to the goals of federal broadband expansion initiatives, which set ambitious timelines for connecting unserved households, as evidence that a faster, more standardized permitting process is needed nationwide rather than left to the discretion of thousands of individual local governments.

## What Happens Next

The proposal is still working through the FCC's formal rulemaking process, which typically involves public comment periods where local governments, industry groups, and the public can weigh in before any final rule is adopted. Legal challenges are considered likely if a final rule is issued, given long-standing debates over the extent of federal authority to override local control of public rights-of-way.

For now, the fight over the 120-day clock reflects a broader and recurring tension in U.S. infrastructure policy: balancing the goal of faster, more affordable broadband deployment against the traditional role of local governments in managing what happens on their own streets. How that balance gets struck could shape not just how quickly new broadband lines get built, but who ultimately has a say in approving them.

*This article is for general informational purposes and reflects the state of a proposed federal rulemaking process, which may change as it moves through further review.*

items.title: 50 Minutes, One War: Inside Rubio and Lavrov's High-Stakes New York Meeting on Ukraine
items.body:
## A Rare Face-to-Face on the Sidelines of the UN

On the margins of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov sat down for roughly 50 minutes — their first direct, in-person talks in months focused squarely on how the war in Ukraine might end.

Diplomats rarely get long stretches of uninterrupted time during the whirlwind of the UN's annual high-level week, so a nearly hour-long session between the top diplomats of Washington and Moscow stood out. Neither side released a detailed transcript, but the meeting itself — happening at all, in person, after a long stretch of strained or indirect contact — was read by observers as a signal that both capitals still see value in keeping a direct channel open, even as fighting continues on the ground in Ukraine.

## The Backdrop: A Day After Trump Met Zelenskiy

The timing was hard to miss. The Rubio-Lavrov meeting came just one day after President Trump met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy in the same city. Taken together, the two meetings amounted to a burst of shuttle diplomacy playing out almost simultaneously in New York — American officials engaging Kyiv one day and Moscow's top diplomat the next.

That sequencing is not accidental. UN General Assembly week routinely becomes an informal hub for exactly this kind of diplomacy: with so many foreign ministers and heads of state already gathered in one place, it offers a rare, low-friction opportunity for meetings that might otherwise take weeks to arrange through formal channels.

## What Was — and Wasn't — Said

Both sides have historically kept these sessions close to the vest, and this meeting was no exception. Public readouts tend to be brief and carefully worded, often describing talks as "frank," "substantive," or "useful" without revealing specific proposals on the table. Given the sensitivity of any discussion touching on territory, security guarantees, sanctions, or a potential ceasefire framework, it's typical for neither Washington nor Moscow to negotiate in public.

What can be said with more confidence is the context: this is the first sit-down of its kind between the two men in months, following periods where contact was limited to phone calls, lower-level meetings, or messages relayed through intermediaries. The mere fact that a meeting of this length happened suggests both sides judged there was enough substance to discuss to justify the time.

## Why This Matters for the War's Endgame

Any durable resolution to the war in Ukraine will require, at minimum, alignment — or at least mutual understanding — between Washington and Moscow on the broad contours of a settlement, even as Kyiv and its European partners remain central to any actual terms. That's part of why meetings like this one draw outsized attention: they're less about producing an immediate breakthrough and more about testing whether the diplomatic groundwork for one exists.

Analysts caution against reading too much into any single meeting. Talks of this kind have occurred before without translating into a ceasefire or broader deal, and deep disagreements — over territorial claims, security guarantees for Ukraine, and the pace or conditions of any troop withdrawal — remain unresolved. Still, the fact that Rubio and Lavrov were willing to spend nearly an hour together, right after high-profile US-Ukraine talks, suggests the diplomatic track around the war is still active rather than frozen.

## What Comes Next

Neither side has publicly committed to a fixed timeline for follow-up talks. In past cycles of US-Russia diplomacy over Ukraine, meetings like this have been followed by working-level contacts between officials tasked with hashing out technical details, though progress has often been slow and uneven.

For now, the takeaway from New York is more about signal than substance: two men who represent countries on opposite sides of the war's diplomacy sat across a table from each other for nearly an hour, a day after the American president met Ukraine's leader in the same city. Whether that translates into real movement toward ending the war remains, as always, an open question — one that will likely only be answered in the weeks ahead as both sides decide whether to build on this conversation or let it fade into the long list of talks that didn't lead anywhere.

items.title: [Retailing 101 #5] Why the Same Gallon of Milk Costs Four Different Prices
items.body:
> Department stores, supercenters, convenience stores, and specialty shops aren't bigger and smaller versions of the same idea — they're four different answers to the question "what is the shopper standing here actually trying to do?"

## Today's Concept

Retailers get sorted by **format** — the recurring bundle of choices a store makes about what it carries, how much help it gives you, and what it charges. Retailing textbooks (Levy & Weitz is the standard one) classify formats along four levers:

1. **Variety** — how many different *categories* the store carries. Also called breadth. Milk, socks, motor oil, and a TV under one roof is high variety.
2. **Assortment** — how *deep* it goes inside one category. Also called depth. Forty running shoes in eleven widths is high assortment.
3. **Service level** — how much labor the store spends on you. Someone measuring your inseam is expensive; a self-checkout kiosk is not.
4. **Price and margin** — what all of the above costs to run, and therefore what it costs you.

No store maxes out all four. That's the whole point. Every format is a deliberate trade.

**Department store** (Macy's, Nordstrom, Dillard's, Kohl's): high variety *and* decent depth, organized into walk-through departments — apparel, beauty, home, accessories. High service, high margin, slow inventory turnover. Historically the format sold the *experience* of shopping as much as the goods.

**The big box — supercenter and warehouse club** (Walmart Supercenter, Target, Meijer; Costco, Sam's Club, BJ's): maximum variety, thin service, low price. A Walmart Supercenter runs roughly 180,000 square feet and stocks well over 100,000 items — general merchandise plus a full grocery. A warehouse club goes the opposite way on depth: Costco deliberately carries only a few thousand items, one or two brands per need, sold in bulk from pallets, funded partly by an annual membership fee (about $65 for a basic card). Fewer choices → bigger orders per item → better cost from suppliers → lower shelf price.

**Convenience store** (7-Eleven, Wawa, QuikTrip, Circle K): tiny variety, tiny depth, tiny footprint — typically around 2,500 square feet and a few thousand items. What it actually sells is *time and proximity*. There are well over 100,000 of them in the U.S., a majority attached to fuel. Merchandise margins are high — roughly a third on in-store goods, far above a supermarket — because nobody price-shops a 90-second stop.

**Specialty store** (Sephora, Foot Locker, REI, Best Buy, Home Depot): narrow variety, extreme depth. One category, done exhaustively, with staff who know it. When a specialty store gets big enough to dominate a category outright, it earns the nickname **category killer**.

Underneath all four sits one arithmetic identity that explains most retail behavior:

```
retail profit engine = gross margin × inventory turnover
```

You can win on fat margins and slow-moving goods (Nordstrom), or thin margins and goods that fly off the shelf (Costco, supermarkets). What you cannot do is run thin margins on slow inventory. That combination is how chains die.

One honest caveat: the boundaries leak. Drugstores sell milk, supermarkets sell flowers, and c-stores sell hot pizza. The industry term for it is **scrambled merchandising** — formats grabbing categories outside their original lane in pursuit of turnover.

## In Everyday Life

Follow one gallon of milk through a normal American week.

**Monday, 7:10 a.m.** You're already late. You pull into the Circle K by the interstate ramp, grab coffee and a gallon, and you're back in the car in four minutes. Say it rings up around $5.29. You didn't compare anything. You paid for the store being ninety seconds off your route and for a clerk being awake at 7 a.m.

**Saturday, 10 a.m.** Costco. Two gallons banded together for roughly what one and a half cost on Monday, plus the $65 membership you already sank in January. You walked past pallets, there were maybe two brands of milk, and you bagged nothing. That's depth traded away for price.

**Saturday, 11:30 a.m.** Target, because you also need socks, a floor lamp, a birthday card, and a prescription. Milk here is somewhere between the other two. You're not buying the cheapest milk — you're buying **one stop**. Variety is the product.

**Sunday afternoon.** Your cousin's wedding is in three weeks and you need a suit that fits. You go to Nordstrom, a person puts a tape measure on you, marks the hem, and the store holds the jacket for a week. Nobody at Costco is doing that. You will pay for it in the price, and the store will hold that jacket in inventory for months before selling it.

**Tuesday evening.** You want *good* trail runners. Not "shoes" — trail runners, for a specific arch. You go to a running specialty shop or REI, where one category fills the whole store and the person on the floor asks how many miles a week you run.

Five errands, five formats, and every one of them was the right choice for the mission it served. Buying the suit at Costco or the emergency milk at Nordstrom would both be errors — the same kind of error, in opposite directions.

## Three-Line Recap

1. A retail format is a bundle of four decisions — variety, assortment, service, and price — and no format wins on all four at once.
2. Department stores buy you breadth plus service, big boxes buy you breadth plus price, convenience stores buy you time, specialty stores buy you depth and expertise.
3. Every one of them survives on the same equation — margin times turnover — and formats constantly poach categories from each other to keep the turnover side up.

## ✅ Self-Quiz

**Q1.** In retailing, "assortment" refers to which of the following?
- (a) The total number of different product categories a store carries
- (b) The depth of choices offered within a single category
- (c) The store's square footage
- (d) The ratio of full-time to part-time staff

**Q2.** Costco carries only a few thousand items while a Walmart Supercenter carries well over 100,000. This mainly reflects a difference in strategy, not a failure by Costco. (O / X)

**Q3.** A convenience store charges more for the same gallon of milk than a supermarket does primarily because:
- (a) Its milk is a higher grade of product
- (b) It is legally required to price above supermarkets
- (c) Its customers are buying proximity and speed, and its small scale carries higher cost per item sold
- (d) It buys milk from different farms

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Retail format** — the recurring combination of variety, assortment, service level, and price that defines a type of store.
- **Variety (breadth)** — how many distinct product categories a retailer carries.
- **Assortment (depth)** — how many choices — brands, sizes, styles — a retailer offers inside one category.
- **Scrambled merchandising** — a retailer adding categories outside its traditional lane, which blurs the lines between formats.
- **Inventory turnover** — how many times a year a retailer sells through and replaces its stock; the counterweight to gross margin.

---

*Answers: **Q1 — (b).** Assortment is depth within a category; breadth across categories is "variety." **Q2 — O.** Costco's limited item count is the mechanism of its low prices: fewer SKUs means larger orders per item, better supplier costs, and simpler operations. **Q3 — (c).** The milk is the same product. You are paying for location, hours, and speed, plus the higher per-item cost of running a 2,500-square-foot store — which is why in-store merchandise margins at convenience stores run far above supermarket levels.*
